title: Kittl Pricing 2026: Plans, Tokens and Export Limits
summary: Kittl pricing is based on three subscription tiers, but the actual cost depends on how many credits you use, not just the monthly fee.
body_markdown:
## Where Activepieces Fits for Repeat Design Work


If you're one person on one plan, you can skip Activepieces, which won't lower your Kittl bill or do any of the designing, though its free plan costs $0 and includes 1,000 credits a month if you want to try it anyway.


Where it earns a look is a team turning out many similar designs, where the cost is people shuffling files and messages between steps.


Picture the shuffling. Someone fills in a request, someone else copies it into a design file, and a reviewer gets asked by chat whether it's ready. The finished exports land wherever the designer happened to save them.


None of that's design. It's hand-carrying, and it's where work gets lost: a brief sits unread, a reviewer never hears the file's done, an export ends up on a desktop.


Do nothing about it and you pay in delays and redone work, which is the same kind of hidden cost as running out of credits halfway through a project.


### How the automation sits around Kittl


Activepieces's an MIT-licensed automation platform with 750 integrations that connects the apps you already use, so that one step triggers the next.


The picture below shows the arrangement: a brief form triggers an Activepieces flow, deterministic steps and a human-in-the-loop approval run, and a reviewer is notified.


The designing itself happens in Kittl; if Kittl isn't in the integration catalogue, you'd need to check for a integration or generate a private one for it.


Every Activepieces plan, the free one included, allows unlimited flows, so the arrangement doesn't depend on a paid tier.


Activepieces meters the run, not the steps inside it: its published pricing page lists 1 credit per flow run, any number of steps, so a ten-step flow costs the same as the two-step workaround it replaced, whereas Zapier's pricing page bills per task and Make's per module.


Splitting the brief, the handoff and the reviewer notice into small separate steps is the sound way to build this, and here it costs nothing extra. Those credits are Activepieces's own and never touch Kittl's tokens.


Because Kittl's plan's set by AI credits and export or commercial-use limits, an automated flow doesn't get you around either one. A flow that kicks off more designs still spends the credits and exports those designs use.


Automation makes it easier to burn through your allowance faster, if anything, so size your plan for the volume you're planning before you wire anything up.


The test is simple. If you're handing the same kind of job between several people every week, automating those handoffs is worth an afternoon of setup. If you're the only person touching the file, a folder and a checklist'll do the same job for free.
